entries.title: Melting of Greenland ice sheet could release methane 'fire ice'
entries.content: Seismic surveys and sediment cores suggest that dozens of deep pockmarks on the sea floor were created when Arctic methane stores were disrupted by climate change after the last glacial maximum – and scientists warn it could happen again

entries.title: Suzanne Simard on the wood wide web, connectedness – and Avatar
entries.content: Rowan Hooper met ecologist Suzanne Simard under an oak tree in Kew Gardens, London, to talk about her new book, criticism of her work, and getting a call from James Cameron's people

entries.title: Neanderthals treated a dental cavity by drilling into the tooth
entries.content: A Neanderthal tooth shows clear signs of human intervention to treat bacterial decay, showing that the earliest dentistry began at least 59,000 years ago

entries.title: Arctic fires are releasing carbon stored for thousands of years
entries.content: A study of soils around the Arctic and boreal forests has found that some wildfires are releasing carbon stored over millennia, meaning higher CO2 emissions than assumed

entries.title: Asteroid set to fly very close to Earth
entries.content: Asteroid 2026JH2 has enough mass to wipe out a city and will zoom past Earth next week

entries.title: Ancient teeth hint at links between Denisovans and Homo erectus
entries.content: Six teeth roughly 400,000 years old have yielded some of the first ancient proteins thought to belong to Homo erectus, providing molecular clues to their relationships with other hominins

entries.title: Natural sunscreen found in fish eggs can be made by E. coli factories
entries.content: Genetically altered bacteria can synthesise gadusol, a naturally occurring compound found in zebrafish eggs that could be developed as an alternative to existing sunscreen products that can harm marine life

entries.title: New rules confirm public has a right to see how UK government uses AI
entries.content: Government departments and other public bodies in the UK must consider requests to release information about AI-produced content, regulators have confirmed. The move follows a successful request by New Scientist for the release of a minister's ChatGPT logs

entries.title: PCOS has been officially renamed PMOS, and it’s a momentous move
entries.content: PCOS will now be known as PMOS (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome), and for Alice Klein, who has the condition, it's been a long time coming

entries.title: Why do particle physicists like spending time in fields?
entries.content: The concept of a field plays a key role in particle physics, but what exactly is it? From its origins in the study of magnetism to the quantum fields of today, columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein goes exploring

entries.title: Carbon credits are flawed, but they can still help save forests
entries.content: Carbon credits bought by companies to offset their emissions really have reduced deforestation, but not by as much as credit developers claim, according to a rigorous analysis

entries.title: A new tectonic plate boundary could be forming in southern Africa
entries.content: Gases collected from boiling mineral springs in Zambia contain the chemical signature of having come directly from the Earth’s mantle, a sign of a rupture in the tectonic plates and the possible beginning of a new continental boundary

entries.title: The story of the first human tool: the humble container
entries.content: An analysis of ancient human artefacts finds that the container, a simple but critical tool, may have originated 500,000 years ago. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how slings, ostrich eggs and wooden trays helped our ancestors survive

entries.title: Can floating data centres meet AI's huge energy demand?
entries.content: A US start-up is putting autonomous data centres in the ocean, powered by wave energy, but experts warn that the harsh environment could make maintenance challenging

entries.title: Huge study of ancient British DNA reveals only minor Roman influence
entries.content: Genetic analysis of 1039 people buried in Britain between the Bronze Age and the Norman conquest highlights the impact of the Romans, Anglo-Saxons and Vikings on the island’s ancestry

entries.title: David Attenborough is one of a kind, for better or worse
entries.content: People often ask who might replace the nature broadcaster, who turns 100 this week. The truth is that he’s irreplaceable, but a wide range of voices are attempting to fill his shoes.

entries.title: Red-light therapy does have health benefits but not the ones you think
entries.content: Red-light therapy promises to treat everything from acne and hair loss to depression and chronic pain. Many of these claims are overhyped, but evidence suggests it can have healing powers

entries.title: Tiny 'metajets' could use light to steer sails for interstellar travel
entries.content: Minuscule silicon wafers propelled by lasers could be used to steer light sails, helping them travel beyond the solar system

entries.title: The 50-year quest to create a quantum spin liquid may finally be over
entries.content: Creating quantum entanglement inside a solid material is tricky in the lab – but crystals buried in the earth could be growing it naturally. Now one scientist says he has proof he’s found them

entries.title: There has been a sudden increase in the rate of sea level rise
entries.content: Satellite measurements show that in the early 2010s sea level rise suddenly accelerated to a rate of 4.1 millimetres per year, possibly in response to an increase in the rate of global warming

entries.title: A vast dam across the Bering Strait could stop the AMOC collapsing
entries.content: If a key ocean current collapses it could plunge northern Europe into a big freeze. Now researchers are weighing up a drastic intervention – building a 130-kilometre-wide dam between the US and Russia

entries.title: A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began
entries.content: A long-overlooked writing system from 5000 years ago is still largely undeciphered, but could mark the moment humans first represented their speech with written words

entries.title: Neanderthal 'kneeprint' found next to mysterious stalagmite circle
entries.content: An impression made in clay around 175,000 years ago could be a kneeprint left by one of the builders of a strange stalagmite circle found deep inside Bruniquel cave in south-west France

entries.title: US government releases huge batch of UFO files
entries.content: The US Department of Defense has released hundreds of documents and photographs related to UFOs, some of which have been declassified, in the first of many drops to come

entries.title: Doubling their genomes may have helped plants survive mass extinctions
entries.content: Many flowering plants have duplicated genomes, which could have helped them evolve to deal with extreme stress in times of environmental upheaval

entries.title: Fire is spreading in the Chernobyl exclusion zone after drone crash
entries.content: A drone has crashed in the Chernobyl exclusion zone, causing a fire that has spread to 12 square kilometres of land. Dry weather, strong winds and the presence of land mines are complicating efforts to bring the blaze under control

entries.title: Slow breathing can calm the mind without any need for mindfulness
entries.content: How important is thinking about your breath for calming yourself down? We now know that slow breathing is effective even without conscious involvement

entries.title: PCOS postpones perimenopause and allows pregnancies at older ages
entries.content: Only 3 per cent of those with polycystic ovary syndrome reach perimenopause by the age of 46, which may allow them to conceive when older

entries.title: New Scientist recommends Attenborough documentary Making Life on Earth
entries.content: The books, TV, games and more that New Scientist staff have enjoyed this week

entries.title: The mathematician who doesn’t exist
entries.content: A secret society of French mathematicians has been revolutionising the field of mathematics under a pseudonym for nearly a century. Columnist Jacob Aron finds that this mythic collective provided maths a rigorous and useful foundation, and did some real harm along the way

entries.title: Former Soviet scientific megastructures captured in striking photos
entries.content: Eric Lusito crossed the former Soviet Union to explore vast scientific sites, some of which have been deserted for years, for his new book

entries.title: Hantavirus outbreak will not cause a covid-style pandemic, says WHO
entries.content: The World Health Organization sought to quell worldwide fears over the hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius and reassure the public that the risk of widespread transmission is low

entries.title: Coffee's mood-boosting effects aren't just down to caffeine
entries.content: A comprehensive study exploring coffee’s physiological effects finds that some of its benefits are down to polyphenols and their influence on gut bacteria

entries.title: What to read this week: the excellent Beyond Belief by Helen Pearson
entries.content: Solving society's problems with evidence is a work in progress, argues a must-read new book. The process is surprisingly new – and riddled with complexities, finds Michael Marshall

entries.title: Where has the deadly hantavirus come from and how does it spread?
entries.content: Three passengers on the cruise ship MV Hondius have died due to an outbreak of hantavirus, a rare illness transmitted by rodents

entries.title: The best new popular science books of May 2026
entries.content: A guide to walking, a look at the world’s Google searches and a deep dive into the secrets of our DNA are some of the topics tackled by the popular science books out this month

entries.title: Less nostalgia, more pain: scientists study 1763 Eurovision songs
entries.content: Feedback discovers that the prevailing themes of Eurovision songs may come and go, but the urge to win stays the same.

entries.title: What to read this week: The 21st Century Brain by Hannah Critchlow
entries.content: Our brains need to adapt quickly to meet the challenges of our digital world, but a rigorous new book by a neuroscientist brings hope that we can do it, says Graham Lawton

entries.title: Pressure from individual particles measured for the first time
entries.content: A device made using a tiny bead floating in a beam of light can measure extremely small pressures and could help find a mysterious kind of neutrino

entries.title: Dating over 50 is probably on the rise – but we know little about it
entries.content: Research into dating has until now almost exclusively focused on younger people, but we’re finally beginning to investigate how romance changes in later life

entries.title: Bronze Age Britons fashioned copper-mining tools out of old bones
entries.content: An analysis of 150 artefacts from a site in Wales shows that the ancient practice of making tools out of bone persisted even after the advent of metal-working

entries.title: Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s
entries.content: At least 15 per cent of the Amazon has already been lost, and further destruction could unleash widespread rainforest dieback with as little as 1.5°C of global warming

entries.title: Huge landslide in Alaska caused 481m-high tsunami
entries.content: When the slope of a mountain above Tracy Arm fjord, in Alaska, gave way on 10 August 2025, 64 million cubic metres of rock fell into the fjord, causing a 5.4 magnitude seismic event

entries.title: Robin Wall Kimmerer's Braiding Sweetgrass is still an essential read
entries.content: This 2013 book by an Indigenous botanist is a quietly urgent act of healing that forces Western science to look at the world in a different way

entries.title: Read the winner of this year’s Young Science Writer Award
entries.content: Prize-winning young writer Hasset Kifle, 17, explores how the world of super-competitive running is being transformed by so-called “super shoes” – and what cost this will have on the sport

entries.title: Extinct relative of koalas discovered in Western Australia
entries.content: Fossils reveal that there were at least two kinds of koala when humans first arrived in Australia, but one died out about 30,000 years ago when the west of the continent dried out

entries.title: Backlash builds over NHS plan to hide source code from AI hacking risk
entries.content: NHS England is pulling its open-source software from the internet because of fears around computer-hacking AI models like Mythos. Opposition is growing among those who say the move is bad for transparency and efficiency, and will also do nothing to improve security

entries.title: Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case
entries.content: A biopsy of a woman's cancer seems to have triggered an immune response against the tumour, putting her into remission

entries.title: The problem of cosmic inflation and how to solve it
entries.content: One of the best-performing models in cosmology is also one with the least physical rationale behind it. Columnist Leah Crane says this leaves us with a puzzle that could make or break physics as we know it

entries.title: Man destined for Alzheimer's may have been saved by accidental therapy
entries.content: Doug Whitney has a genetic mutation that means he should have developed Alzheimer’s disease decades ago, but his long-term work in hot engine rooms may have protected him in a similar way to sauna therapy

entries.title: Quantum computers simulated their biggest molecule yet – with help
entries.content: Two quantum computers and two supercomputers teamed up to break the record for the biggest molecule yet to be simulated using quantum hardware

entries.title: Honey has been used as medicine for centuries – does it really work?
entries.content: It is appealing to think something as simple as honey could cure a cold or prevent hay fever, but is there evidence to back up honey’s health benefits? Columnist Alice Klein finds that it has legitimate medicinal uses, depending on the type of honey you’ve got

entries.title: Tiny frozen world unexpectedly appears to have an atmosphere
entries.content: A 500-kilometre-wide object in a similar orbit to Pluto challenges our assumptions about small bodies in the outer solar system

entries.title: 300-year-old experiment could become world's best dark matter detector
entries.content: An update to an experiment run by Henry Cavendish in 1773 could be a cheaper and faster way to spot a potential dark matter particle – and may be 10,000 times more sensitive

entries.title: An unorthodox version of quantum theory could reveal what reality is
entries.content: The implications of quantum mechanics suggest reality isn't as solid as we think it is, but physicist David Bohm had a spin on the theory that restores reality. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan explores how we could test Bohmian mechanics – and if it will ever become more widely accepted

entries.title: The greatest David Attenborough documentaries you really need to watch
entries.content: To mark David Attenborough turning 100, New Scientist staff have been set a tricky task: pick your favourite of his many amazing documentaries...

entries.title: Prebiotic chewing gum could be helpful for gum disease
entries.content: A small trial found that chewing gum containing nitrate can ease the symptoms of gum disease by favouring the growth of beneficial mouth bacteria

entries.title: Smart underwear detects lactose intolerance by tracking your farts
entries.content: A device you attach to your underwear reveals how often you really break wind – and it’s probably more frequently than you think

entries.title: Why dinosaurs lived much more complex lives than we thought
entries.content: A wave of dinosaur discoveries over the past decade has completely reshaped our understanding of these long-extinct animals. Palaeontologist Dave Hone spills the secrets of how dinosaurs lived, from how social they were to how much they really fought

entries.title: Is consciousness more fundamental to reality than quantum physics?
entries.content: The idea that everything that exists can be built from the bottom up has long held sway among physicists. Now, a new kind of science is under construction that centres conscious experience – and might unravel the universe’s biggest mysteries

entries.title: Our verdict on Red Mars: Mostly great, with a few quibbles
entries.content: The New Scientist Book Club read Kim Stanley Robinson's acclaimed science fiction story about the first settlers on Mars in April – and had a lot to say about it

entries.title: Ann Leckie continues to shine with new sci-fi novel Radiant Star
entries.content: Set on a planet whose population lives underground, Radiant Star is Ann Leckie's latest Radch-universe novel. Its rich characterisation and meticulous world-building shine through, says our science-fiction columnist Emily H. Wilson

entries.title: 2026 will be the hottest year on record, leading scientist predicts
entries.content: The second half of this year will almost certainly see the start of an El Niño phase that could lead to extreme heat across much of the globe, and James Hansen expects that to make this year surpass 2024 as the hottest on record

entries.title: Why the keto diet could be a revolutionary way to treat mental illness
entries.content: You may think of the high-fat, low-carb eating plan as a faddish way to lose weight. But the keto diet is now being used to tackle conditions from severe depression to bipolar disorder and anorexia, with transformative results

entries.title: The mysterious reason why women get hotter from age 18 to 42
entries.content: Women experience a steady rise in body temperature from their teens to midlife, which may be useful for monitoring ageing and overall health

entries.title: Can we harness quantum effects to create a new kind of healthcare?
entries.content: Experiments hint that quantum mechanisms are vital to the machinery of life. Now researchers are exploring if these effects help to explain the success of an array of puzzling health treatments

entries.title: We could generate hydrogen from rocks while storing CO2 in them
entries.content: Storing carbon dioxide in rocks while producing hydrogen from them - and perhaps even geothermal power too - could be a double win on the climate front, and several groups are trying to make it happen

entries.title: Embryos made without sperm or eggs reveal why many pregnancies fail
entries.content: Embryo organoids made from stem cells are enabling scientists to recreate early pregnancy in the lab, unlocking treatments for infertility, miscarriage and pre-eclampsia

entries.title: Wealthy people with environmental ideals are the biggest emitters
entries.content: Among people of high socioeconomic status, love for nature corresponds with a bigger environmental footprint – and there's an obvious reason why

entries.title: NASA plans a base on the moon spanning hundreds of square kilometres
entries.content: Three missions slated to launch this year will begin to search the lunar surface for a suitable base location

entries.title: First quantum grandfather clock could probe where gravity comes from
entries.content: Researchers have designed a quantum version of a pendulum clock. It could shed light on timekeeping in the quantum realm

entries.title: We may finally know why gold stays so shiny
entries.content: Gold is chemically inert and so doesn't tarnish, but exactly why had been a mystery

entries.title: How a radical new view of life could reveal its origin – and aliens
entries.content: We've been looking at nature the wrong way, argues Rowan Hooper. If we stop focusing on the individual, we get a whole new picture of how life on Earth – and elsewhere – may have begun

entries.title: Space storms could switch train signals and cause serious accidents
entries.content: Critical safety equipment in many train systems is vulnerable to disruption by space weather, which could lead to fatal accidents

entries.title: Earliest use of anaesthetics uncovered in Chinese doctor’s tomb
entries.content: Residues on medical equipment reveal that physicians in China over 600 years ago used aconitine, a highly toxic plant chemical, to alleviate pain during surgical procedures

entries.title: Will lab-grown sperm let infertile men have children of their own?
entries.content: Men who do not produce sperm can’t be helped by existing fertility treatments, but a start-up is now claiming it can grow their sperm in the lab. Columnist Michael Le Page suspects this technique will have to be combined with gene editing if it is to help many men

entries.title: Attack on Iran’s oil released as much pollution as a volcano
entries.content: Airstrikes on Tehran earlier this year emitted a plume containing almost 30,000 tonnes of sulphur dioxide that reached Asian countries

entries.title: Does gravity create reality? A shocking path to a theory of everything
entries.content: A rewrite of quantum mechanics that includes the force of gravity could finally achieve one of physicists’ biggest goals and reveal the ultimate fuzziness of time

entries.title: PMOS shows us why many scientific terms need to be renamed
entries.content: Like covid-19 and mpox before it, the decision to relabel PCOS as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome is a welcome one – and reveals why a name is never just a name

entries.title: Mars astronauts may do laundry by blasting clothes with a plasma beam
entries.content: There is currently no good way for astronauts in space to do laundry, but researchers may have finally come up with one: a bright purple jet of microbe-killing plasma

entries.title: Why your brain needs plenty of “Aha!” moments
entries.content: In the age of AI, instant answers to our questions are readily available. But columnist Helen Thomson finds that continuing to encourage those delicious flashes of insight that come from your own thoughts may be beneficial both for your everyday life and your long-term brain health

entries.title: Epic dreaming is leaving people exhausted and distressed
entries.content: Some people experience vivid, incessant dreams that leave them feeling exhausted the next day, with researchers calling for this "epic dreaming" to be classed as a sleep disorder

entries.title: Women’s better memories may delay Alzheimer’s diagnosis by years
entries.content: Women appear cognitively normal for almost three years longer than men after their brains start to develop Alzheimer’s disease, making it harder to diagnose and preventing early treatment

entries.title: This is the most underrated sci-fi film franchise of the 21st century
entries.content: There’s unexpected news of a fifth movie for one of the most underrated sci-fi reboots. Hurray, says New Scientist film columnist Bethan Ackerley

entries.title: Mercury may have gained all of its unexpected water in a single day
entries.content: Despite being the closest planet to the sun, Mercury has thick deposits of ice at its poles, and now we may understand the events that formed them over just one Mercurian day

entries.title: Experimental mRNA vaccine may protect against multiple Ebola viruses
entries.content: Tests with rodents suggest an mRNA vaccine in development offers protection against three strains of Ebola virus, including the one behind the current crisis

entries.title: Mathematicians stunned by AI's biggest breakthrough in mathematics yet
entries.content: Artificial intelligence built by OpenAI has cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, which mathematicians have hailed as a monumental moment for AI in mathematics

entries.title: Photos reveal unexpected details from the world's first atomic test
entries.content: Previously classified photos and documents show the scientific work that went into the world's first atomic test in 1945 – a test that, just weeks later, would see nuclear bombs dropped in Japan

entries.title: Political anger affects the body differently to other forms of anger
entries.content: We all feel emotions like anger and disgust from time to time, but they seem to cause stronger bodily sensations when they're politically induced

entries.title: Australia is battling its largest diphtheria outbreak in living memory
entries.content: Vaccine misinformation, nurse and doctor shortages and crowded living arrangements may be behind soaring rates of diphtheria in remote Indigenous communities in Australia

entries.title: How a visit to Stonehenge reminded me of deep time
entries.content: On a visit to the UK, Sydney-based reporter James Woodford visited an archaeological site that was on his bucket list – and experienced a very special moment as the sun set

entries.title: How ageing on Earth mimics the effects of space travel
entries.content: Life on the International Space Station may feel distant, but columnist Graham Lawton finds that studying how astronauts experience accelerated ageing could help us fight similar effects on Earth related to sedentary lifestyles, disrupted circadian rhythms and social isolation

entries.title: New Scientist recommends a devastating account of farming honeybees
entries.content: Jennie Durant's Bitter Honey is a great exposé of the true cost of industrially farming US honeybees, finds Thomas Lewton. But the book's grim figures of bee death alone may not prompt deep change – how about seeing them as fellow creatures?

entries.title: Shiver me timbers: Do we have to worry about space pirates now?
entries.content: Feedback goes down a "moon warfare" rabbit hole and discovers that some forward-thinkers are making plans to counteract as-yet-hypothetical pirates in space

entries.title: Women’s body temperature rises from age 18 to 42 but we don’t know why
entries.content: Women experience a steady rise in body temperature from their teens to midlife, which may be useful for monitoring ageing and overall health

entries.title: Putting CO2 into rocks and getting hydrogen out is climate double win
entries.content: Storing carbon dioxide in rocks while producing hydrogen from them - and perhaps even geothermal power too - could be a double win on the climate front, and several groups are trying to make it happen

entries.title: Flotation tanks deployed to combat PTSD after devastating wildfires
entries.content: Maui in Hawaii experienced some of the worst wildfires in US history in 2023. Amid concerns of a PTSD epidemic, flotation tanks are being deployed to the island to help restore people's mental health

entries.title: Everyone is Lying to You for Money is a must-watch exposé of crypto
entries.content: Actor Ben McKenzie explores the world of crypto in an entertaining documentary that doesn't shy away from calling out those who have promoted the currency

entries.title: The maths meme that has been distracting mathematicians for a century
entries.content: A seemingly simple set of rules kicks off a kind of mathematical magic trick, which has kept great minds busy since the 1930s. Columnist Jacob Aron explores the origins of the Collatz conjecture, why it is so addictive to mathematicians and whether AI could help us solve it once and for all

entries.title: Escher: The paradoxical artist beloved by mathematicians
entries.content: A new retrospective of M.C. Escher’s work opens this week. Explore some of his most mind-bending, mathematically inspired works here

entries.title: Becoming a parent may make you love your partner less
entries.content: Parents report loving their partners less within the first year of having a child, but that doesn't mean the feeling is permanent or inevitable

entries.title: Mysterious ‘cold blob’ in the Atlantic suggests the AMOC is weakening
entries.content: A patch of ocean south-east of Greenland is the only place on Earth that is cooling, and it could be a sign that the warm water "conveyor belt" in the Atlantic is slowing down

entries.title: How Rachel Carson's Silent Spring changed the world in 1962
entries.content: Rachel Carson’s look at the dire effects of industrial and agricultural pollution birthed the modern environmental movement when it was first published – and remains as crucial a read today, finds Rowan Hooper

entries.title: The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come
entries.content: Global warming will amplify the impacts of El Niño events, and could also make them much stronger and more far-reaching

entries.title: Stonehenge's altar stone probably wasn't transported by a glacier
entries.content: A glacier could have carried the giant sandstone at the centre of Stonehenge southwards from north-east Scotland, but this scenario appears unlikely

entries.title: New Scientist recommends a deep dive into our organs by Giulia Enders
entries.content: Giulia Enders made her name with Gut, an exploration of our intestines. Now, in the compelling follow-up Organ Speak, she’s listening to what our other organs are telling us

entries.title: Is there a word for the Wiki page for the Ship of Theseus paradox?
entries.content: Feedback has been flooded with answers (both correct and inspired) after wondering if there is a word for something that is an exemplar of the thing it describes.

entries.title: Earth has a mysterious triple symmetry that may influence its climate
entries.content: A circle running along the 27° east and 153° west meridians divides the globe into two halves with equal reflectivity – and this may have implications for solar geoengineering schemes

entries.title: Ditch the niceties in AI prompts to save energy use, say researchers
entries.content: A UN report warns of the rapid growth in AI energy consumption, but suggests users can improve efficiency by making prompts more concise

entries.title: Atom-based quantum computers are catching up in the race to usefulness
entries.content: A quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms can correct its own errors during long computations, an important prerequisite for becoming truly useful

entries.title: Keto diet shows real promise for anorexia recovery
entries.content: Restricting carbohydrates may sound like an unlikely approach to treating anorexia, but following a ketogenic diet was linked to recovery in nearly 75 per cent of people with the eating disorder in a small trial

entries.title: Ötzi's frozen remains may harbour metabolically active microbes
entries.content: Researchers studying a 5300-year-old mummified man have identified bacteria that lived in his gut when he was alive, as well as cold-tolerant fungi that colonised his body after death

entries.title: Why you need to future-proof your brain in middle age and how to start
entries.content: Ages 40 to 65 see a period of turmoil in the brain that has previously been overlooked. But identifying problems during this time can protect your cognitive health for decades to come

entries.title: How the electromagnetic spectrum opened our eyes to the universe
entries.content: Our understanding of the electromagnetic spectrum goes back to Isaac Newton, but astronomers are still finding new ways to employ it. Astrophysicist Emma Chapman explores how much these invisible waves can reveal to us about the cosmos – and whether they might show us that we’re not alone

entries.title: The best new popular science books of June 2026
entries.content: The most exciting popular science reads this month explore everything from symbiosis to hormones, while Alice Roberts takes on an editor-in-chief role in her latest book

entries.title: CERN’s new chief on the gamble that could fix our picture of reality
entries.content: Mark Thomson has taken the reins at CERN just as particle physics confronts some of its deepest unknowns – and faces hard choices about what comes next

entries.title: Hearing loss is bad for the whole body – but new treatments are coming
entries.content: From dementia to heart attacks, hearing loss has been linked to a wide range of effects across the body, and the condition is on the rise. Fortunately, we're learning how best to safeguard this crucial sense and how we might be able to reverse the damage

entries.title: Hidden store of manganese may have helped Earth get its oxygen
entries.content: Computer simulations have uncovered a new manganese compound that could exist deep in Earth’s mantle and may be connected to the process that gave our atmosphere oxygen

entries.title: New Scientist recommends Togetherness, a radical new view of life
entries.content: An exploration of how biological cooperation underpins all life - and why we’ve overlooked its power until now - makes thrilling reading, finds Penny Sarchet

entries.title: A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out
entries.content: Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

entries.title: 'Transformative' pancreatic cancer drug doubles survival time
entries.content: People with advanced pancreatic cancer taking an experimental daily pill lived nearly twice as long as those receiving chemotherapy infusions

entries.title: How human error became a weapon against large language models
entries.content: Alan Turing proposed a test for machine intelligence: could a computer convince a human it was human? We have begun conducting the same test on ourselves, writes Max Moser

entries.title: Do turmeric and curcumin have any actual health benefits?
entries.content: Turmeric is heralded for its anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory properties, but columnist Alice Klein finds that the evidence for this is shaky. Taking high doses of its curcumin extract in supplement form can be risky

entries.title: Huge study of Alzheimer’s genetics identifies new drug targets
entries.content: Almost 50 more genes have been flagged as being linked to Alzheimer’s, along with changes in activity in crucial cells that disappear as dementia progresses

entries.title: Capitalism has warped our understanding of ecology and life’s origins
entries.content: The ideas of survival of the fittest and winning at all costs are closely entwinned with Darwinism, but they shouldn’t be. A rethink from a more communal perspective is in order

entries.title: Geoengineering can thicken Arctic sea ice, but for how long?
entries.content: Two companies are aiming to preserve Arctic ice by pumping water onto the sheet and letting it freeze, but only one of the trials found that this delayed melting in the summer

entries.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
entries.content: A cancer-killing virus has stopped pancreatic tumours from growing and spreading in three people in an initial safety trial, raising hopes that it may help to beat the deadly condition

entries.title: The best new science-fiction books of June 2026
entries.content: There is plenty of intriguing sci-fi on offer this month, whether it’s solar-powered cities from Adrian Tchaikovsky or a strange future from M. John Harrison

entries.title: Photons behave very strangely if you try to cut them
entries.content: Particles of light cannot be divided into smaller particles, but if you try to snip off the end of one, instead of shortening it multiplies

entries.title: Our verdict on Luminous by Silvia Park: a fascinating take on robots
entries.content: The New Scientist Book Club read Silvia Park's near-future sci-fi novel Luminous in May, and had lots of good things to say (along with a few complaints)

entries.title: The late Ian Watson's sci-fi The Embedding is intriguing – but dated
entries.content: Watson's death last month prompted sci-fi columnist Emily H. Wilson to read his acclaimed 1973 debut and find out what she'd been missing. She found it fascinating – but reflective of its time

entries.title: Glaciers in the 'roof of the world' have suddenly started melting
entries.content: Until recently, the Pamir mountains in central Asia have bucked the global melting trend, but in 2025, the region’s glaciers experienced a massive loss of ice due to extreme heat

entries.title: Aim high but don't shoot for the moon, mathematicians advise
entries.content: According to a mathematical model of how people weigh up different outcomes, the optimal strategy is to be ambitious, but not overly so

entries.title: Horror video game gets its creepiness from a quantum computer
entries.content: Quantum Backrooms is a horror game in which the player explores eerie rooms. The twist is that the rooms have been generated by a quantum computer

entries.title: Mirror life: Scientists clash over threat of lab-engineered bacteria
entries.content: Bacteria created using mirror images of natural biomolecules would pose a grave threat to life on Earth, some researchers warn, but a new study suggests they would struggle to survive in the wild

entries.title: We're becoming more individualistic and it's affecting our love lives
entries.content: We're increasingly prioritising our own needs over those of the wider community, which may be causing us to love our partners less intensely

entries.title: Read an extract from The Selfish Gene by Richard Dawkins
entries.content: Dive into the opening of The Selfish Gene's first chapter 'Why are people?', the New Scientist Book Club’s read for June to mark 50 years since the popular science classic was first published

entries.title: Unsettling dance piece explores how AI is warping human relationships
entries.content: Inspired by Shannon Vallor's book The AI Mirror, this compelling piece looks at how we are being affected by our deepening interactions with tech

entries.title: Q-Day could destroy bitcoin – and our retirement savings
entries.content: Even if you’ve never bought any cryptocurrency, like columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan, your money may be affected by bitcoin’s fate – which is uncertain, as quantum computing advances are threatening to make the encryption protecting it useless

entries.title: Earth from Above author returns with astonishing freshwater images
entries.content: From Kenya's Tree of Life to a Svalbard glacier, these stunning photos are taken from a new book by Yann Arthus-Bertrand, whose The Earth From Above was a smash hit 25 years ago

entries.title: Mathematical AI helps researchers crack 50-year-old problem
entries.content: After an AI from OpenAI found a trick to solve an 80-year-old conjecture from Paul Erdős, mathematicians have borrowed the same technique to solve another important problem

entries.title: Start-ups are racing to revolutionise mathematics with AI
entries.content: AI start-ups with hundreds of millions of dollars in funding are hiring mathematicians and building AI systems that they hope will not only solve mathematics, but also build more intelligent AI

entries.title: 3D-printed lymph nodes could widen access to CAR T-cell therapy
entries.content: The cost of CAR T-cell therapy means that the highly effective cancer treatment is unavailable in many parts of the world. But a new way of making these cells could dramatically drive down the cost

entries.title: 'The book is in the future, but everything is seeded from our present'
entries.content: Helen Phillips, winner of the Climate Fiction prize for her novel Hum, on if stories can make a difference, her anxieties and writing about the climate

entries.title: Millions of planets might form around supermassive black holes
entries.content: Massive amounts of dust swirl around active nuclei at the centres of galaxies, and these discs could give rise to vast numbers of rocky planets, some even the size of stars

entries.title: New Scientist recommends Turi King's expert book about DNA's secrets
entries.content: From clearing people convicted of murder to identifying a monarch's remains, Michael Le Page is fascinated by The Secrets of Our DNA, an insider's must-read book

entries.title: Cuts to US ocean programme will hinder monitoring of El Niño and AMOC
entries.content: Scientists warn that the Trump Administration's push to dismantle a vital network of ocean sensing instruments will stymie crucial weather and climate monitoring in the Pacific and Atlantic

entries.title: Flood of AI 'garbage' is pushing open-source developers to the limit
entries.content: The modern world depends on open-source software maintained by volunteers, but the added demands of checking and fixing AI-written submissions are causing some to burn out and quit

entries.title: A chromosome from a frozen rat has been resurrected inside mice
entries.content: Mice that contain cells with an added rat chromosome have been created by scientists. The next step is to try this with frozen elephant tissue – and if that works, the team will try it with frozen mammoths
